comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
Fixed on branch `drift-fd2b-eebc`, commit `d043be48dcba`, pushed for review with `chiselled-glandulous-fantail` (shared file).

## What landed

`scripts/check_terraform_tree_currency.py` — a portable, three-valued currency gate, plus a hard (non-advisory) invocation of it in the drift workflow's `plan` job **before** `terraform plan`, and a section in `infra/runbooks/provision-restore.md` for the local operator.

Against the ACs:

- **AC1** — the verdict is three-valued and named: `0 CURRENT`, `1 STALE`, `2 UNKNOWN`. The stale message states in full that a plan from this tree answers a different question, that declared-but-absent resources read as "No changes", and that deleted-but-still-present resources are proposed for RECREATION. So "your tree is stale" is not merely a different exit code from "infrastructure matches", it is a different sentence. A test asserts that sentence is present rather than only asserting the exit code.
- **AC2** — currency is established from a **fresh `git fetch <remote> <branch>`**, compared against `FETCH_HEAD`, never from anything in the working tree. A tree missing the newest declarations cannot also make the remote tip look like itself. The anti-defeat property is pinned as a CONTRAST, not an assertion: on the same fixture, `--no-fetch` (which trusts the clone's own `origin/main`) wrongly reports the stale clone CURRENT, while the default fetching path reports it STALE. `UNKNOWN` is a distinct third state precisely so an unestablished currency is never collapsed into "current" — that collapse is how this bug class gets made.
- **AC3** — asserted, not assumed. The `plan` job runs the gate before `terraform plan`, without `continue-on-error`, so the sweep cannot reach a verdict without having planned the tracked tip. Mode is `tip` for the scheduled/dispatched sweep and `ancestor` for a pull request (whose checkout is a merge commit that CONTAINS the base tip rather than being it — a PR built on a stale base still fails). `actions/checkout` gained `fetch-depth: 0` because a shallow clone cannot reach a merge base; a test pins that too, since losing it would silently degrade every run to `UNKNOWN`.
- **AC4** — defect-seeded in `tests/unit/test_terraform_tree_currency.py` using real temp git repositories: origin declares a second alarm, a clone taken before it is shown STALE, and the control (a clone at the tip) is GREEN from the same fixture. The reverse direction is seeded separately — a clone that predates a deletion — because that is the dangerous one. Divergence (a local commit) is seeded too and reports `diverged from` rather than `behind`.
- **AC5** — plain Python + `git`. No CI provider, no terraform binary, no AWS call, no network beyond the git remote. A developer runs the identical script the workflow runs; documented in the runbook with the exit-code contract.

## What I deliberately LEFT OUT, and why

**The local half is DETECTABLE, not UNAVOIDABLE.** The check is available and documented locally, but nothing *compels* an operator who types `terraform plan` or `terraform apply` directly to have run it. That is a real residual gap and I am not calling this ticket's AC5 more than it is: AC5 asks that the check *works* with no CI provider, which it does; it does not ask that local terraform be *wrapped*, and the ticket's own non-goals say the requirement is that staleness be VISIBLE, not that stale runs be forbidden.

Making it unavoidable locally needs a different mechanism — a `make tf-plan` / wrapper entry point, or a shell function, that runs the gate and then execs terraform — and that is a separate design question (which entry point, what happens when someone bypasses it, whether a wrapper that can be bypassed is worth the mechanism it adds against the mechanism-delta ratchet). I did not fold it in here because it would change the shape of the fix rather than extend it, and because a half-committed wrapper is exactly the kind of "mechanism that looks like enforcement" this repo is trying to stop growing. **Filed as a sibling ticket, linked `discovered_from` this one** — see the linked ticket.

Nothing was applied. `terraform apply` remains operator-only; the workflow plan stays `-lock=false -detailed-exitcode`, read-only.

comments.body:
Pushed for review: **Gerrit change 2658** — https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/c/rebar/+/2658 (commit `1748404108c3`, branch `drift-fd2b-eebc`). Shares the change with `chiselled-glandulous-fantail`; both ids are in `rebar-ticket:` trailers.

Sibling ticket for the residual local-enforcement gap: `naptunium-ethnologic-bighorn` (`6863-077f-f091-46b1`), linked `discovered_from` this ticket.

One design tradeoff worth recording, since it is a deliberate choice to fail loudly rather than tolerate: if `main` advances between the plan job's checkout and the currency step's fetch, HEAD is a strict ancestor of the fetched tip and the step reports STALE — a false red. The alternative is a tolerance window, which is a second mechanism whose entire job is to let some staleness through, i.e. the exact failure this ticket exists to close. A rare, loud, investigable red is the right side of that trade; the reasoning is written into the workflow next to the step so a future reader does not "fix" it into a fudge.

Local state before push: `make lint` green (both ratchets `new=0 increased=0`), `make typecheck` green, full `make verify` suite green after the mechanism-baseline entries were added.

Not closing — waiting on `LLM-Review +1` and `Verified +1`, and the operator submits.

compiled_state.description:
## The hazard

`terraform plan` run from a checkout that is behind `origin/main` reports **"No changes"** for
resources that are declared on `main` but absent from the local tree. That output is
indistinguishable from the healthy case, so an operator or agent reads "infrastructure matches
declaration" when the truth is "this tree does not contain the declaration".

## Observed, 2026-09-05

The main checkout at `/Users/joeoakhart/rebar` was **14 commits behind `origin/main`**.
`monitoring_autodeploy.tf` there was 355 lines with 6 alarms; on `origin/main` it is 624 lines with
11. Running `terraform plan` from that checkout returned 91 `resource_changes`, **all `no-op`** —
`Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy`.

Five CloudWatch alarms from epic 6202 stories S2 and S3 were declared on `main` and **did not exist
in AWS**. Confirmed independently with `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms` before the apply. An apply
from the stale tree would have succeeded, changed nothing, and been reported as done.

Running the same plan from a tree at `origin/main`, against the same S3 remote state, returned
`Plan: 5 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy`.

## The worse direction

Under-application is the benign failure. The dangerous one is the reverse: if a future commit
**removes** a resource, an apply from a tree that predates that commit proposes **recreating** it —
so a stale checkout does not merely fail to converge, it can actively undo intended deletions.
Neither direction produces a warning.

## Why this belongs with tonight's other findings

It is the same class that has recurred repeatedly in this repo: **an operation that did not happen,
reported as success.** The Terraform Drift workflow was blinded for two days by a whitespace defect
before `plan` ever ran (`chiselled-glandulous-fantail`); a CI job cast a passing vote without
executing; a probe silenced itself and its absence read as health. Here the plan genuinely ran and
genuinely found nothing — because it was asked the wrong question.

Note the drift workflow has the same exposure: `terraform-drift.yml` fails on a non-empty plan, so
it is only meaningful if it runs against current `main`. If it ever ran from a stale ref it would
report clean for exactly this reason.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] AC1 - A Terraform plan or apply executed against a tree that is behind the tracked branch is
      DETECTED and reported as such, distinctly from "no changes needed". A reader must be able to
      tell "your tree is stale" from "infrastructure matches".
- [x] AC2 - The check is not defeated by the stale tree itself — i.e. it does not rely solely on a
      file that the stale tree also lacks.

      CURRENCY MECHANISM (decided here, not deferred to the executor): fetch the remote ref
      FRESH and compare the local HEAD against it -- never read a pre-existing local
      remote-tracking ref, which the staleness being detected can itself have left behind.
      Two modes: `tip` (HEAD must equal the fetched tip) for the scheduled sweep, and
      `ancestor` (the fetched tip must be an ancestor of HEAD) for a PR merge commit.
      The result is THREE-valued -- current / stale / could-not-establish -- because
      collapsing the third state into either of the other two is how this bug class is made.
      Checkout must be full-depth: a shallow clone has no merge base and would silently
      degrade every run to could-not-establish.
- [x] AC3 - The daily drift workflow provably runs against current `main`, and that is asserted
      rather than assumed.
- [x] AC4 - Defect-seeded: reproduce the observed case (a tree behind `main` whose plan is empty
      while `main`'s is not) and show the check fires. A check that would not have caught the
      2026-09-05 instance has not been shown to work.
- [x] AC5 - Portable per `project.portability`: works for a developer running terraform locally with
      no CI provider, not only inside a workflow.

## Non-goals

Not preventing local terraform runs from a feature branch — that is legitimate. The requirement is
that the staleness is VISIBLE, not that it is forbidden. Not fixing the fmt-before-plan ordering,
which is `chiselled-glandulous-fantail`.

## Note on the local checkout specifically

This ticket is about the missing SIGNAL, not about one checkout. The checkout can be fast-forwarded
by its operator at any time; it was deliberately NOT fast-forwarded during this incident because
AGENTS.md forbids fast-forwarding the shared main checkout (it may hold uncommitted operator WIP)
and because other agents were actively working against it.
